chapter.title: Kicking from the hips

cards.body: You are lying on the bed again, face down this time, with your legs hanging off the end. Now swing them from the hip, lazily, the way a kid swings their legs on a tall chair. That lazy swing is the whole kick. **Small, from the hips, feet just under the surface.** The bed keeps holding you. The legs only add a push.
cards.simpler: Lie on your bed, face down, with your legs hanging off the end. Now let them swing from the hip, slow and lazy, like a kid swinging their legs on a tall chair. That lazy swing is the whole kick. **Small, from the hips, feet just under the surface.** The bed holds you up. Your legs only add a little push.

cards.prompt: Two people push off the wall at the same time. Maya kicks hard, knees pumping, water flying a metre in the air. Sam's feet barely dimple the surface with quick little flicks. Who is further along when they both stand up?

options.text: Maya. More splash means more power.
Sam. Small flicks from the hip push the water backwards, not upwards.
About the same. The kick barely matters in front crawl.

whyNot.a: That's noise, not push: water thrown into the air has left the pool, so it can't move you forward.
whyNot.c: That's true of a bad kick, not a good one: a small hip kick is what keeps your legs up and lets the arms do their job later.

cards.reteach: Think of a fish's tail. It never leaves the water and it never bends in the middle. A kick that stays under the surface pushes water behind you, and water behind you means you go forward. Splash is the push escaping.

cards.title: Where the kick starts
cards.body:
**The kick starts at the hip, not the knee.** Your whole leg swings like a long pendulum. The knee stays soft, bending only a little, the way it does when you walk.

Ankles go floppy. A loose ankle lets the foot flap like a flipper, and the flipper is what actually pushes the water. A stiff, pointed-hard foot cuts through the water and pushes nothing.

Keep it small. Your feet move about 30 cm apart, top to bottom, and the heels just break the surface. Start by holding the pool edge with both hands, lying flat, face in, and kicking for 10 seconds.
cards.simpler:
**The kick starts at the hip, not the knee.** Your whole leg swings like a long pendulum. Keep the knee soft. It bends only a little, like when you walk.

Let your ankles go floppy. A loose foot flaps like a flipper, and the flipper is what pushes the water. A stiff foot cuts through and pushes nothing.

Keep the kick small. Feet move about 30 cm apart, heels just breaking the surface. Start by holding the pool edge with both hands, face in, kicking for 10 seconds.

cards.title: Ten seconds at the wall
cards.body:
Hold the edge with both hands, arms long, and let your legs float up behind you. Blow your bubbles, then start the small swing from the hips. Count 10 seconds in your head.

Now the test. If the water behind you goes white and foamy, your kick is too big. If the lifeguard glances over to see what the noise is, it is much too big. A good kick is quiet enough that you can hear your own bubbles.
cards.simpler:
Hold the pool edge with both hands, arms long, and let your legs float up behind you. Blow your bubbles, then start the small swing from the hips. Count to 10 in your head.

Now check. If the water behind you turns white and foamy, your kick is too big. If the lifeguard looks over to see what the noise is, it is much too big. A good kick is quiet. You should still hear your own bubbles.

cards.prompt: You are holding a kickboard, face in, kicking. After 5 metres your legs have sunk and you have stopped moving. What is most likely going on?

options.text: Your knees are bending a lot, so you are pedalling instead of swinging from the hip.
Your ankles are too loose and need to be held stiff.
The kickboard is the wrong size for you.

whyNot.b: That's the fix for the opposite problem: loose ankles are what you want, because the floppy foot is the flipper.
whyNot.c: That's the equipment, not the kick: any kickboard floats enough, and sinking legs come from the knees, not the board.

cards.reteach: When the knee bends a lot, the foot comes forward and down, and the hips drop with it. Sinking legs are almost always a knee kick. Straighten the leg, keep the knee soft, and swing the whole thing from the hip.

cards.title: Why big kicks lose
cards.body:
A big kick bends the knee, and a bent knee drags your foot down through the water like an anchor. Your hips drop, your legs sink, and now you are kicking uphill. **The small kick keeps your body flat on the bed.**

Steady beats fast. Aim for a rhythm you could keep for a minute, not a sprint that dies in 5 seconds. If you are out of breath after one width, slow the kick down.

Build it in three steps: holding the wall, then holding a kickboard, then from a push-off glide with no board. Face in, breathe out, and lift your chin forward to breathe when you need to, then put your face straight back in.
cards.simpler:
A big kick bends the knee. A bent knee drags your foot down through the water like an anchor. Your hips drop, your legs sink, and now you are kicking uphill. **The small kick keeps your body flat on the bed.**

Steady beats fast. Pick a rhythm you could hold for a minute, not a sprint that dies in 5 seconds. Out of breath after one width? Slow down.

Build it in three steps: hold the wall, then a kickboard, then glide with no board. Face in, breathe out, lift your chin forward to breathe, then face back in.

cards.body: Dev got on the kickboard and started cycling, knees up to his chest, feet churning like he was late for a bus. He went nowhere, slowly, and then slightly backwards. Spot it in yourself this way: if your knees are coming up toward your tummy, you are pedalling. Straighten the legs until the swing comes from the hips, and the board will start to move.
cards.simpler: Dev got on the kickboard and started cycling. Knees up to his chest, feet churning like he was late for a bus. He went nowhere, slowly, and then a little backwards. Here is how to spot it in yourself: if your knees come up toward your tummy, you are pedalling. Straighten your legs until the swing comes from the hips. Then the board starts to move.

cards.prompt: Which of these describes the kick this chapter wants?

options.text: Legs locked rigid and straight like two planks, toes pointed hard, kicking as fast as you can.
Swung from the hips, knees soft, ankles floppy, feet just under the surface, steady rhythm.
Big kicks from the knee that splash high so you can feel the power.

whyNot.a: That's stiff, not soft: locked knees and hard-pointed toes turn off the flipper and tire you out in seconds.
whyNot.c: That's the knee kick that sinks your hips, not the hip kick: the splash is the push leaving the water.

cards.reteach: Three words: hips, floppy, small. The swing comes from the hips, the ankles stay floppy so the feet flap like flippers, and the kick stays small enough that the water behind you stays quiet.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Kick from the hips with soft knees and floppy ankles, small and steady, feet just under the surface.** Big splashy knee kicks drag your legs down and move you less, so quieter is faster.
cards.simpler: **Kick from the hips with soft knees and floppy ankles, small and steady, feet just under the surface.** Big splashy kicks from the knee drag your legs down and move you less. A quiet kick is a faster kick. If you can hear your own bubbles, you are doing it right. Think of a lazy leg swing, not a bicycle.

cards.body: Tonight, lie face down on your bed with your legs off the end. Swing them from the hips for 20 seconds, knees soft, feet relaxed. If your knees bend a lot, that is the pedalling to unlearn.
cards.simpler: Tonight, lie face down on your bed with your legs off the end. Swing them from the hips for 20 seconds. Keep your knees soft and your feet relaxed. Watch your knees. If they bend a lot, that is the pedalling habit you need to unlearn. The swing should come from the hip, like a long pendulum.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now kick a small, steady flutter kick from the hips across the width of the pool holding a kickboard, with your face in the water and your breath going out.
